characterization_methods.purpose: Measure austenite content and (for QA specimens) obtain SFE parameters.

characterization_methods.key_findings: δ-ferrite begins to precipitate at ~1485 °C; austenite forms by peritectic reaction (δ-F + L → A) at ~1390 °C; at ~970 °C austenite fraction reaches a maximum (~91.4 %) while δ-ferrite is minimum (~8.6 %); the A1 (cementite precipitation) temperature is ~617 °C.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: equilibrium phase fraction and phase-composition vs temperature
characterization_methods.purpose: Calculate the phase volume fraction diagram of the present steel to justify quenching/intercritical annealing temperatures.

characterization_methods.key_findings: IQ-1050: YS 575 ± 13 MPa, TS 929 ± 30 MPa, TE 2.0 ± 0.3 % (poorest ductility among all specimens).
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: room temperature; strain rate 0.375 min^-1; rod-shaped M10*60 mm specimen, gauge length 25 mm; tensile axis parallel to the rolling direction
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure tensile properties of IQ-1050 (YS, TS, TE).

computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: Alloy composition Fe-8.9Mn-4.6Al-0.29C (wt.%) with P, S < 0.005 wt.%; temperature range ~500-1600 °C
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: The calculated dual-phase (δ-ferrite + austenite) window and A1 ≈ 617 °C were used to select the 1050 °C quenching temperature and the 620/680/740/800 °C annealing temperatures.

analytical_models.model_note: KAM_ave = exp((1/N) Σ ln KAM_i); ρ_GND is GND density of the calculated area, KAM_ave the average local misorientation.

computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: EBSD step size μ = 150 nm; Burgers vector b = 2.887 Å for BCC and 2.563 Å for FCC (measured by XRD)
computational_details.simulation_method: GND density calculation from EBSD kernel average misorientation (KAM)
computational_details.software_used: HKL Channel5 software and Python (EBSD data analysis)
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Computed BCC and FCC GND densities of IQ-1050 compare with values reported for strained Hadfield austenitic steel (~9.80 ×10^14 /m^2 at true strain ~0.05).

interfaces.interface_notes: Heating to 1050 °C largely decreased the GND density of the hot-rolled microstructure, but considerable martensitic transformation during quenching caused volume expansion, still resulting in high GND densities of lath martensite and retained austenite.
interfaces.phase_evolution: During holding at 1050 °C all martensite in the hot-rolled steel reversed into austenite; C and Mn diffusion into austenite increased the austenite volume fraction, giving more lath martensite at room temperature. Prior austenite grains grew up and prior austenite grain boundaries (PAGB) moved to δ-ferrite, thinning and segmenting the δ-ferrite bands into discontinuous grains. The high heating temperature lowered the Mn content of the reversed austenite, decreasing austenite stability and raising Ms; the higher cooling rate of water quenching than air cooling further inhibited α-ferrite transformation and raised Ms, so the martensite region of IQ-1050 was larger and retained austenite fewer at room temperature.

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: After intercritical quenching, the yield strength of IQ-1050 (~575 MPa) was improved compared with HR, but tensile strength declined (~929 MPa vs HR ~1107 MPa) and total elongation was the poorest of all specimens (~2.0 %), indicating premature failure.

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: 5 kg vacuum-induction-melted ingot heated to 1100 °C for 2 h prior to forging. Depicted as the homogenization plateau in Fig. 1.
The homogenized ingot was forged into a square forging ingot measuring 80 mm × 70 mm.
The forging ingot was reheated to 1100 °C and held for 2 h before hot rolling.
Hot rolled from 80 to 12 mm thickness in eight passes; thermomechanical rolling in the dual-phase region produced the micro-laminated δ-ferrite/martensite structure.
processing_steps.reduction_ratio: from 80 to 12 mm thickness in eight passes
processing_steps.temperature: initial rolling temperature approximately 1050 °C; finishing rolling temperature approximately 950 °C

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Hot-rolled plate air cooled to room temperature; the resulting hot-rolled sample was labeled HR, which is the parent state of IQ-1050.

processing_steps.method: intercritical reheating (austenitization in ferrite + austenite dual-phase region)
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: The hot-rolled plate was reheated to 1050 °C, located in the ferrite and austenite dual-phase region, and held for 1 h. 1050 °C was selected as quenching temperature because around 970 °C the austenite fraction reaches a maximum (~91.4 %) and, allowing for Thermo-Calc discrepancy, 1050 °C makes the austenite volume large enough.

Water quenching of the 1050 °C reheated plate; the corresponding sample was labeled IQ-1050. The higher cooling rate of water quenching than air cooling inhibited α-ferrite transformation and increased the Ms temperature, giving a larger martensite region and fewer retained austenite.

measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: rod-shaped sample size of M10*60 mm, gauge length 25 mm; tensile axis parallel to the rolling direction of the hot-rolled plate

tensile_properties.stress_strain_curves: Engineering stress-strain curve for IQ-1050 shown in Fig. 5(a) (curve labelled IQ-1050); peaks near 900 MPa at ~2 % strain as read from the figure.

structures.overall_structure: Micro-laminated (banded) microstructure inherited from the hot-rolled state (heredity), consisting of δ-ferrite bands and a lath martensite region; before quenching the plate was held in the ferrite + austenite dual-phase region at 1050 °C, so prior austenite grains grew and the δ-ferrite bands became thinner and were partly divided into discontinuous δ-ferrite grains. The martensite region of IQ-1050 was larger and retained austenite fewer than in HR.

unmapped_findings: IQ-1050 yield-to-tensile ratio = 0.62 and product of strength and elongation (PSE) = 1.9 ± 0.4 GPa % (Table 3).

For IQ-1050, the density of block boundaries (boundaries with misorientation > 45°) was higher than that of austenitic grain (AG) boundaries, in contrast to HR; this increased block-boundary density contributed to the yield strength of IQ-1050, and the red block-boundary bar density was highest at IQ-1050 (a little above the 0.8 µm^-1 gridline) among all conditions (Fig. 8(b)).

IQ-1050 had a poorer tensile strength (929 ± 30 MPa) and ductility (2.0 ± 0.3 %); more lath martensite in IQ-1050 than HR contributed to its higher yield strength (575 ± 13 MPa) but readily induced stress concentration during deformation causing premature failure.
The GND densities of austenite in HR and IQ-1050 were similar (FCC ~8.37 ×10^14 /m^2 for HR and ~5.01 ×10^14 /m^2 for IQ-1050).
